for_you_if: you enjoy patient sandbox automation and building
you play with split screen partners locally

you need online matchmaking instead of split screen
you expect a helpful introductory tutorial

claims.claim: Reviewers report that multiplayer is limited to Steam Remote Play with split-screen rather than featuring native online matchmaking.

citations.review_text:
The game doesn't offer multiplayer, only "shared/split screen multiplayer", which is an insult to all players.
It's not the 2000s anymore. People have Internet nowadays.

I bought Hydroneer because I wanted a factory game to play with my friend. It started up and ran great in single-player. Once we got Steam Remote Play working, we had to use the required split-screen mode that this company forces, which dropped my resolution to 1080p. Which doesn't matter, the game is pretty low quality, so it wasn't a huge deal. However, after about 40 minutes, the game completely froze, and I had to force restart my PC just to get out of it. When my computer started back up, it was still stuck at 1080p and was using my CPU's integrated graphics instead of my dedicated GPU. Somehow, this game ended up corrupting the AMD drivers for my 7900 GRE. I reinstalled the drivers, and everything is working again now, but I have already submitted a refund request for the game.

I hear the actual gameplay is fun, but I only bought it to play multiplayer with a friend and the multiplayer SUCKS. It is the worst multiplayer system I have experienced, requiring steam remote play, which means it will be split screen.

Don't buy this if you want to play with your friends!
Online multiplayer only works over remote play, that means one person streams his games to all the other players, everyone sees a full split screen view and only one person can use mouse and keyboard.
Apart form that i like the idea of the game but since I don't want to play the game alone i can't rate the game positively.

Yeah, so... If you're looking to play this game with a friend/friends, unfortunately, it's splitscreen/Steam remote play only, which we didn't know beforehand, not having read the reviews. My friend saw it and recommended it for us to play and subsequently bought it for the both of us. We played through the tutorial, really liked the concept, only then realizing as we were getting ready to play together, that it was splitscreen only. Which, really wouldn't be a problem, if it wasn't Steam remote play, streaming the game to one another and having network fluctuations nearly constantly, effecting the gameplay to a practically unplayable degree. It certainly seemed fun and my best friend and I were excited to give it a shot, being fans of Deep Rock Galactic and all, but... Yeah, if you were looking for a regular online co-op game, that isn't the case for this, as of now, at least. Fingers crossed, they'll release non-splitscreen sometime, but until then... I don't know, maybe give Deep Rock Galactic a shot if you're a fan of similar games. -- Recommended for solo, but for any sort of multiplayer outside of couch co-op, this isn't quite the one.

seen a video on this game and it looked cool until I went to play with my friends. we are in 2026 and it is using split screens for coop? really?
the game looks and acts fine, its just not what I wanted it for.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that items drop to the right of the crosshair rather than where the player is aiming, making precise placement difficult.

citations.review_text: what the hell is the point of a reticle if nothing lines up with it without extra input?

Moving items (a basic and necessary action) is terrible. There is no way to be sure where something you are holding will be put. If objects attracted items when dropped, that wouldn't be a problem, but they don't. Nothing is dropped where your crosshairs are looking, but somewhere to the right of it. The tutorial quickly made me realize this is not a mining or sandbox game. It is a puzzle game and hidden object finder -- because you will be trying to work out where things can go and find things you dropped.

The early game is pretty miserable. As others have pointed out, you can only carry one object at a time, which makes everything a little tedious. Even worse, you have to precisely place some objects into other objects, and most of these placements do not line up with the aiming dot, but instead some vague region off to the right of it. How is the mid and late game? I have no idea, and will not find out.

I'm fine with the weird inventory system (meaning buckets and carts... there is no inventory system in this game), but nothing is ever dropped where my cursor is. It always drops things toward the bottom right of the screen, so I have to line everything up there, move until its out of sight, THEN drop. I'm on a 3440x1440 monitor, so maybe that's why? But my resolution doesn't cause issues in any other way. Sadly, this genuinely makes the game unplayable. I can't be bothered to drop every single item 5+ times to get it right. And there is a LOT of dropping things into a specific spot in this game. A cursory web search shows that one can hold E to move the item where the cursor is, THEN drop with more precision, but that raises the question: Why even have the default method of dropping?

For a game about only being able to hold one item at a time, you would think dropping items, holding items in containers, and placing stuff would be a polished experience?
Nope! Money clips through the pan and lands on the surface beneath. Trying to load a bunch of ore in a pot is tedious because you don't place stuff where you looking, you place below your right hand. Hidden the settings is a switch to turn on a laser sight so you can see where you are dropping it, but even with this, Minecraft has better "drop held item" than this game. The worst thing is that the shovel is both to good and really bad at detecting dirt; When you try to scoop up dirt, it misses, you have to click around till the collision finds a cell or something stupid (i have never seen a digging game this bad at digging). When you try to drop the shovel, suddenly the floor is in the way and there is simply no room to drop your shovel on a perfectly flat barren field.
Good prototype, but don't pay for this.

The game seems fun after the early game (as long as your save doesn't delete itself) but getting past the early game is glacially slow and unfun. The lack of QoL (idk like an inventory, a coin purse, or even placing things at your crosshair instead of offset slightly to the right) and any meaningful tutorial makes it not approachable to anyone  who isn't familiar with it prior. The dev has stated that the game is completely finished; and the only updates are from the console team who you will have to hope will add some QoL because I cannot fathom how awful it would feel to try and place anything with the current physics on an anvil or in the pan on a controller.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the controls and item placement mechanics as clunky and difficult to manage.

citations.review_text:
I'll cut straight to the point here: the controls and UI here are VERY clunky and tedious.

If that's the kind of thing that doesn't bother you, then you'll probably find a lot to enjoy here as the systems and interactions seem robust and creative. But I found myself fighting the controls and the lack of an inventory system more than actually dealing with the gameplay itself and that was a real shame.

Again, this is really all down to that one central complaint, so if you're okay with some clunkiness and jank, this could absolutely still be worth trying. Just go in knowing that it's a little rough around the edges.
Very clunky gameplay, just couldn’t get into it.

Started in the tutrial as the game advised to get feel for mechanics/controls but the center screen reticle is actually useless nothing but the stores/picking up items seems to accuratelly reflect where the cursor is, placing items on /in objects you have to use the shadow to reliably put them where you want/need. There's a several year saga of a basic tutorial function being lost in the sauce because despite there being muliple ways to achieve early steps the flow text only updates if you follow the exact wording. So you will almost assuredly miss that to make the ring on the anvil you need to smelt your gold, and then reheat the smelted bar (extermely counter inuitive) and then hit the anvil. 

For me *on controler* the game feel isn't good and the game logic feels needlessly obtuse on top of that so I uninstalled.

Looks bad ad plays bad. 

Just the first basic action of putting something into something else is an ordeal. Controls are unintuitive, even just picking up something.

Low poly graphics always look bad, it's never been a style, it's the law of least effort. Early 3D graphics were trying to do something nice with what they had, nowadays low poly is just an excuse. Also don't like the chunky character models.

The controls are very awkward and there is so much inconvenience. I hate the early game and did not get past it. I saw there were ways to make some mechanics like transporting less inconvenient but it feels like punishment to do it at the start, and not something I can later look back on with joy how I managed to automate it (if that makes sense).

I love automation games, especially first person and crafting types.  Satisfactory is one of my favorites.

I played this game for a bit and absolutely loathed it.  The crafting seems ok and there are some interesting ideas but the UI and controls are so janky and clunky and awkward that it actually made the game wholly unpleasant.  I quit after about half an hour because I just couldn't stand the awkward cursor selections.  In a game like this you should be focused on organizing the next steps, not worried about fighting with the mouse cursor to see if you can actually pick something up.  It was really dreadful.  Very disappointed.

The tutorial I also felt was really quite bad.  It doesn't really tell you what you need to know, or at least I felt that in several cases it just missed really important details.  It also doesn't really explain any of the surrounding info.  It's a generally very low effort tutorial that should have had a lot more thought put into it.

In a game like this, or really in any game, you cannot skimp on the early game effort.  People get 1 to 2 hours to judge a game before refunds expire, and if you can't give a good impression in that time, it doesn't matter how good the game gets later.

I don't even know if this game has potential at mid or later stages because the beginning was just too awful for me to get through, primarily due to the cursor, UI, and control issues above.

claims.claim: The game lacks an inventory system, restricting players to carrying only one item at a time.

citations.review_text:
This game loves to just waste your time. It's a tedious nightmare because you have 0 inventory so you can only hold 1 object at a time. 

I gave it a fair shake and realized I wasn't having fun. Why do I have to carry my coins and put them in a bucket to buy things at a vendor and then go to another vendor across town only to realize I left my coins at the previous vendor. There's a section that you have to walk for a minute and a half each way to a vendor up and down an elevator/stairs. So you bring your coins down, pay for your stuff then bring your item up and then go back down to get your coins back. WHY!?

This game is cool! 

Please for the love of god tighten up the controls a bit. Having to repeatedly pick up and drop something over and over until I aim it in the right spot just to complete an action SU-UCKS. Also please let me carry more than one item. A bag, hot bar, even just two hands worth of items?? I have two hands, I swear I do

EDIT: I'm now several hours in - my god this game is so fun. What a cool execution of a neat concept. Combines some of my favorite aspects of so many different games. Definitely scratches the Satisfactory itch. My "let me hold at least more than one single item" point still stands in my opinion, just seems to unnecessarily slow me down. Otherwise, no complaints so far- having tons of fun!

For a game centered around automation and building no inventory system. One item in your hand at a time is mind boggling in a building game. The game turns more so pick up and put down simulator than anything. Don't get me started on the drop system too. Items can overlap at certain times but have hard collision boxes as well. This game could really use some quality of life changes. -10/10 really wanted to like this game and see its potential but in this day and age I really don't want to play another game that just feels like work. Wouldn't recommend this to anyone to be honest.
No inventory so making anything is a running back and forth simulator and controls are so annoying that there is an item in the game to make it less annoying

I thought this game would start out with a lot of busywork and then slowly get over to the automation fun. And it does...*kinda*. However, a lot of things in this games are just an annoying hassle.

If you drop things, you don't drop them in front of you, but slightly to the right. While a dropshadow indicates where it lands, it's still a massive annoyance, especially because "drop things" is the #1 way of interacting with the world. You cannot, for example, place something in a crucible or on an anvil, you pick it up and drop it.

You can only ever carry one thing at a time, no inventory. This includes money. This means if you go into a shop you need to carry everything out to the cart, one thing at a time. If you dropped a bunch of ores, you pick them up one at a time. And then drop them in the container you want. Which, as I said before, is on the right of the screen, not the center. And yes, some shops are VERY DEEP inside a mountain so you are running back and forth a bunch of times instead of just having an inventory.

Spent a few hours with this and it was enjoyable enough, but I'm done. There is something of a game here, but it tries its hardest to be as unapproachable as possible.

The starting is slow af but after everything is setup the game is so easy , the only thing i don't like is not having inventory , its a pain in the but to carry one thing at a time but overall its a really good game!

Tl;dr: Good enough that I bought it after playing a pirated copy, but it is held back by some truly bizarre design decisions that feel even more frustrating with how obviously the devs possess both skill and motivation.

First, the positives. The game runs brilliantly. I have not yet really pushed things, but my rather modest mining setup runs without a single hiccup on my ancient 4670K. The NPCs and their fetch quests make the game world feel more friendly and alive, which is a pleasant departure from the hostile worlds of Factorio and Satisfactory. I absolutely love the aesthetic. I also love how everything runs on water, and that the devs give you a magic water pumping pipe rather than requiring you to power the water pump. I like how the vehicles are so easy to get back upright after flipping them. I like how you can combine gems into larger ones. And of course, I love the built-in mod support.

For example, aside from a set of basic starting tools, everything you will use has to be bought from shops with money you earn by crafting commodity items like daggers, axes, and jewelry. That itself is fine, but for some reason, the devs think that it is a good idea to have to manually carry your money from shop to shop to buy things which, since you do not have any kind of internal inventory, means either making multiple trips back and forth to carry the money to the shop, bring back each purchase one at a time, and then retrieving your money, or using the in-game pallets which have finite space and take your pace from "a bit slow" to "old man with his shoes tied together." This is partly solved once you get one of the trucks, but even that requires you to cheese things by dropping things from above the truck bed in order to get your various items of cargo to phase into each other.

As others have mentioned, digging mines is a chore, and requires you to either use the shovel to relocate one  basketball-sized piece of soil at a time or use things like explosives or the …

And yes, some shops are VERY DEEP inside a mountain so you are running back and forth a bunch of times instead of just having an inventory.

Jank can be fun, but this isn't the right kind. It's difficult to purchase items, build items, transport items, modify terrain... I see the vision with being without an inventory, but you may have gone too far by not even having a place for money. If the intent of the game is base building, it's too much of a pain to play.

bought the game a few years ago, played for 10 minutes and put it down, recently picked it back up since I got interested again and wondered if the devs fixed the game feel. They didn't. "Hydroneer is a finished product". 

Now, I will probably change the review to positive once I put more hours into the game and things start to get "automated", but for how everything is so poorly executed so far, I can't recommend this. I see the appeal and the vision of the "no inventory", and I respect that, but just because it's a design vision doesn't mean it can be an excuse for poor game polish. Tutorial hasn't been changed for (I think) 3 years, things are still a text wall, cart moving is clunky, and on the topic of clunkiness, the player character. Character needs more friction, I enter a hold that I dug but cannot get out and just keeps slipping, and this happens on normal terrain too, the "unstuck" button just sends me to the underworld and I have to walk all the way back to early game area.

There's often no feedback from when something happens and you NEED to know, things like whether things are in the buckets or not (which the game claims can be used for storage purposes, but guess what, it breaks whenever the bucket is in a cart), when something needs to be rooted instead of just dropped to be used (spent 5 minutes in the TUTORIAL wondering why my anvil doesn't work, turns out I needed to place it, call me dumb I guess but the tutorial should've told me).

All of the points above make me not want to play the game even though the gameplay itself is super fun, having 0 QoL, intentional cripples that may or may not be relieved through gameplay (making a "lock/unlock building" purchasable item instead of just changing the keybind to something more intuitive), and just general lack of polish.

 The core concept of this game is super fun and addictive—it definitely keeps me coming back. That said, it has some rough edges. The UI and controls for dropping items are awkwardly mapped and just feel clunky. The game also does a terrible job of explaining new mechanics, relying on vague picture boards scattered around the map instead of actual instructions.

Let me be very clear: I like the GAMEPLAY of this game; the part where I work to get money and then start to make my manual grindset become automated and I get to watch my creation go to work.
I recommend hydroneer for that.

HOWEVER. This game is a tedious running simulator.
You have to pick up everything one by one. Every tool, every item, every building piece. Everything.
I enjoy setting up my workplaces. I hate how they have to be set up. One by one.
Building a new mine/ refinery line? Here's the step by step process of how to do it :D
1. Go to shop. 
2. Move cart to position. 
3. Spend 10 minutes, one by one, picking up a bunch of pipes and conveyors (this is excluding buying specific items like sorters, smelters, etc. 
4. Buy them and bring them back. 
5. Spend another 15 minutes offloading them and trying to poorly organize them. 
6. Spend another 45 minutes running each individual piece, one at a time, back and forth, until I've completed the assembly line I had in mind.

That's the SIMPLIFIED way of putting it, and I'm being really generous on how much time that actually takes to do; that's not even mentioning the fact that in order to get the miners, you have to bring resources to the forge in Icehelm, forge new miners one by one, and then transport them back and place them one by one.

Final words: 
This is a great game that loses a LOT of points because for some reason, an inventory system, or in the very least the ability to hold more than ONE PIPE (or any building item) at a time is too much.

Good game to play if you hate yourself.

The world is utterly static and lifeless. It feels like driving around a test world, where they haven't added any NPCs or other systems. Moving from point A to B is an utterly pointless exercise in time-wasting tedium.

There's no inventory, which artificially extends the playtime of the game by at least 50%, and keeps you away from the interesting portion of the game by making it too difficult to actually place buildings. Some people find this laudable "WOW NO INVENTORY EVERYTHING EXISTS AS A 3D MODEL SO REALISTIC". It's not realistic, because you can stack things infinitely in a cart, where items clip through each other. 

If this game had a simple inventory system, and purchasable upgrades instead of making them physical items like the "hammer that locks or unlocks items", this would be a legitimately fun automation game. Instead it ends up feeling like a lifeless slog.

So, if you are depressed and hate yourself, buy and play this game. Otherwise, play something actually fun like factorio.

citations.review_text:
It's fun, I like it.
The game mechanics are somewhat weird, but you get used to it. Apparently you only have one hand, but can lift even the heaviest equipment. But once your hand is full (say with some coins), you can't pick up anything else.

And it seems your character has some hand-eye coordination issues - it takes some time to get used to how to drop items.

That being said, it gets quite enjoyable once you've adapted to it. As the title implies, all machinery is water powered (even your truck, heaven knows how), so piping stuff is a core mechanic.
Designing how to lead the pipes, aligning machines next to piping, all that is part of the fun. And much trial and error, and digging - most of the time you're underground and need to clear space to put machines. Since that's hard work, you'll likely try to stay as cramped as possible.

The quests are simple - NPCs demand an item, you provide it. Be it a nugget of a specific size (or bigger) or something more complicated like a sword or a necklace. With specific materials and weights, of course.

The game has two currencies, the "normal" money you earn by selling your spoils directly to a vendor, and the Token, you get from regular NPCs tasks (quests).
The token you need for fancy equipment.

If you don't want to do any quests, but try to create the heaviest gold bar possible - go for it. The game doesn't mind.
(Note that all bars, or compressed gems have a max SIZE, but no max WEIGHT. A bar with a weight of 200 looks no different from one with a weight of 5000.)

Volcalidus:
The DLC, I'll drop a few words about that:
More of the same, which IMO is a good thing. Instead of water, here everything uses lava, but the techniques remain.
Water IS used as well, but this time only for the belts. You have to create your own water, though, because the volcanic island is an ice desert.

All in all it's as much fun as the base game, though unfortunately (to me) it has no end game. While I don't want the game to end, I'd like t…

Ok, this is definitely a niche game.  You have to love go-at-your-own-pace gaming and be willing to set your own goals in a sandbox. It's pretty satisfying for the Minecraft crowd.  
There are quirks, some of them are pretty hard to overcome, like the dropping of held items off-center.  When you eventually get used to this as a feature, you can pick rocks, ore, fish, vegetables up and drop them in your container offset to the side rapidly. Learning to position correctly makes a ton of difference in gameplay quality of life.
Also, you can hold the drop button to instead place the item at your cursor, that can be really helpful for handing off quest requests or precision placement of buckets and the like.  
I've got 100 hours, I'm not done with all the goals I've come up with, I know there's a few other easter eggs out there, but mostly I relax with an audiobook and full buckets with dirt, looking for those rare ores.
This title just received an optimization for 2026, which is really above and beyond for the development team and I was happy to revisit this review given their dedication to the title.

This game has a ton of character and personality. It's a nice change from factory games (3500 hrs. in Factorio ;) and can be very relaxing...

    ... once you get used to the controls. They are very challenging at first, but it really pays off (no pun intended) to stick with it. Lots and lots of really nice little dopamine hits - the sound design, the comic style of flat shading, watching things grow as well as the surprises from digging and mining.

    The water system for energy is clever, too, and along with all of the logic parts you can create some really intricate (and sprawling!) machines.

    There's a definite learning curve (mostly with the controls), but practice, experiment, and just enjoy the world that they've built and [if you like factory games as much as I do!] you'll appreciate how entertaining this sim can be!
